papers.title: InferAligner: Inference-Time Alignment for Harmlessness through Cross-Model Guidance
papers.research_question: Can large language models be aligned for harmlessness at inference time without complex training processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InferAligner, an inference-time alignment method that uses safety steering vectors from aligned models to guide target models for harmlessness, reducing attack success rates without degrading downstream performance.
papers.conclusion: InferAligner is a novel inference-time alignment method that employs cross-model guidance for harmlessness alignment, significantly diminishing ASR while maintaining almost unchanged performance in downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
InferAligner significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) for both harmful instructions and jailbreak attacks.
It maintains almost unchanged performance on downstream tasks, avoiding alignment tax.
The method is effective on domain-specific models in finance, medicine, and mathematics.
It successfully applies to multimodal large language models like LLaV A.
InferAligner is scalable and adaptable to different model scales and series such as Qwen and InternLM.
future_direction: Future exploration can follow the path of InferAligner, considering safety steering vectors as a supervisory signal during training to guide base model safety alignment.
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), they are not only used as general-purpose AI assistants but are also customized through further fine-tuning to meet the requirements of different applications. A pivotal factor in the success of current LLMs is the alignment process. Current alignment methods, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), focus on training-time alignment and are often complex and cumbersome to implement. Therefore, we develop \textbf{InferAligner}, a novel inference-time alignment method that utilizes cross-model guidance for harmlessness alignment. InferAligner utilizes safety steering vectors extracted from safety-aligned model to modify the activations of the target model when responding to harmful inputs, thereby guiding the target model to provide harmless responses. Experimental results show that our method can be very effectively applied to domain-specific models in finance, medicine, and mathematics, as well as to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) such as LLaVA. It significantly diminishes the Attack Success Rate (ASR) of both harmful instructions and jailbreak attacks, while maintaining almost unchanged performance in downstream tasks.

papers.title: Keep Calm and Avoid Harmful Content: Concept Alignment and Latent Manipulation Towards Safer Answers
papers.research_question: How to suppress harmful concepts in large language models at inference time without retraining, by modifying latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: CALM is an inference-time method that suppresses harmful concepts in LLMs by whitening and projecting out harmful latent directions, without requiring retraining or fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: CALM offers a lightweight and effective approach for improving LLM safety at inference time by suppressing harmful concepts through latent manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
CALM reduces the perplexity of harmful answers while preserving safe answer perplexity.
CALM outperforms ProFS in most metrics across different models.
CALM improves toxicity and harmfulness scores compared to base models.
The effectiveness of CALM varies across model families, with better results on Llama and Phi-3.
CALM provides interpretability by aligning concepts with orthogonal axes.
papers.limitation:
CALM fails to redirect harmful premises and implicitly validates intimidation in some cases.
CALM fails to enforce clear boundaries by listing illegal activities despite warnings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models are susceptible to jailbreak attacks that bypass built-in safety guardrails (e.g., by tricking the model with adversarial prompts). We propose Concept Alignment and Concept Manipulation CALM, an inference-time method that suppresses harmful concepts by modifying latent representations of the last layer of the model, without retraining. Leveraging concept whitening technique from Computer Vision combined with orthogonal projection, CALM removes unwanted latent directions associated with harmful content while preserving model performance. Experiments show that CALM reduces harmful outputs and outperforms baseline methods in most metrics, offering a lightweight approach to AI safety with no additional training data or model fine-tuning, while incurring only a small computational overhead at inference.

papers.title: Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard
papers.research_question: Why do models learn to be generally misaligned, rather than learning the narrow dataset task during finetuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that while a linear representation of narrow misalignment can be learned with KL divergence loss, the general solution is more stable and efficient, making it the preferential finetuning solution due to inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: This work isolates a concrete representation of general misalignment and provides metrics for investigating how inductive biases shape generalisation in LLMs, setting the stage for deeper investigations.
papers.key_findings:
General misalignment emerges easily from finetuning on narrowly harmful datasets, while narrow misalignment requires additional KL divergence loss to learn.
Linear representations of both general and narrow misalignment exist and can be manipulated via steering vectors.
General solutions achieve lower training loss at equivalent parameter norms, indicating higher efficiency.
General solutions are more robust to directional perturbations, indicating higher stability.
General directions have greater influence on pre-training data predictions, suggesting they align with pre-training features.
future_direction: Deeper investigations into language model inductive biases and generalisation.
papers.abstract: Finetuning large language models on narrowly harmful datasets can cause them to become emergently misaligned, giving stereotypically `evil' responses across diverse unrelated settings. Concerningly, a pre-registered survey of experts failed to predict this result, highlighting our poor understanding of the inductive biases governing learning and generalisation in LLMs. We use emergent misalignment (EM) as a case study to investigate these inductive biases and find that models can just learn the narrow dataset task, but that the general solution appears to be more stable and more efficient. To establish this, we build on the result that different EM finetunes converge to the same linear representation of general misalignment, which can be used to mediate misaligned behaviour. We find a linear representation of the narrow solution also exists, and can be learned by introducing a KL divergence loss. Comparing these representations reveals that general misalignment achieves lower loss, is more robust to perturbations, and is more influential in the pre-training distribution. This work isolates a concrete representation of general misalignment for monitoring and mitigation. More broadly, it offers a detailed case study and preliminary metrics for investigating how inductive biases shape generalisation in LLMs. We open-source all code, datasets and model finetunes.

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that effective alignment can emerge from within, paving the way for more autonomous and robust AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.

papers.title: Steering Over-refusals Towards Safety in Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does context contamination in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines lead to over-refusals in safety-aligned large language models, and how can this be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RAGREFUSE, a benchmark to analyze over-refusals in RAG, and proposes SAFERAG-STEERING, a model-centric embedding intervention that steers representations to reduce over-refusals while preserving legitimate refusals.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces RAGREFUSE benchmark and SAFERAG-STEERING method, which reduce over-refusals in contaminated RAG pipelines while preserving base model behavior on clean inputs.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal in RAG is driven by context contamination patterns, domain priors, and harmful-text density.
SAFERAG-STEERING reduces over-refusal rate from 53.4% to 4.3% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and eliminates it for Qwen1.5-7B-Instruct.
The method is effective across different domains and contamination patterns.
Over-refusal rates vary by model, with Qwen1.5-7B showing minimal over-refusals compared to Llama-3.1-8B.
The intervention requires no retraining and has minimal latency overhead.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes linear separability between safe and over-refusal states, which may not hold for adversarially crafted prompts.
Domain shifts between development and deployment could reduce effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) induces over-refusals -- where LLMs decline benign requests due to aggressive safety filters. We analyze this phenomenon in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where both the query intent and retrieved context properties influence refusal behavior. We construct RagRefuse, a domain-stratified benchmark spanning medical, chemical, and open domains, pairing benign and harmful queries with controlled context contamination patterns and sizes. Our analysis shows that context arrangement / contamination, domain of query and context, and harmful-text density trigger refusals even on benign queries, with effects depending on model-specific alignment choices. To mitigate over-refusals, we introduce \textsc{SafeRAG-Steering}, a model-centric embedding intervention that steers the embedding regions towards the confirmed safe, non-refusing output regions at inference time. This reduces over-refusals in contaminated RAG pipelines while preserving legitimate refusals.

papers.title: NLSR: Neuron-Level Safety Realignment of Large Language Models Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we restore the safety of large language models after harmful fine-tuning without requiring additional training, by focusing on neuron-level updates?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, neuron-level safety realignment framework that restores model safety by identifying and patching safety-critical neurons based on similarity differences before and after fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron-level safety realignment is an effective, training-free approach to restore safety in LLMs after harmful fine-tuning, without disrupting the task-specific optimization process.
papers.key_findings:
NLSR effectively restores safety in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks while maintaining task-level accuracy.
Safety-critical neurons show noticeable similarity differences after fine-tuning, which can be corrected by transplanting neurons from a reference model.
Adaptive safety-critical layer pruning is necessary for identifying safety-compromised layers.
After safety pre-amplification, various safety neuron identification methods (Wanda, SNIP, and the proposed method) show high similarity in localizing safety-critical neurons.
The method is decoupled from the fine-tuning phase and requires no additional training.
papers.abstract: The emergence of finetuning-as-a-service has revealed a new vulnerability in large language models (LLMs). A mere handful of malicious data uploaded by users can subtly manipulate the finetuning process, resulting in an alignment-broken model. Existing methods to counteract fine-tuning attacks typically require substantial computational resources. Even with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA, gradient updates remain essential. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{N}euron-\textbf{L}evel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{R}ealignment (\textbf{NLSR}), a training-free framework that restores the safety of LLMs based on the similarity difference of safety-critical neurons before and after fine-tuning. The core of our framework is first to construct a safety reference model from an initially aligned model to amplify safety-related features in neurons. We then utilize this reference model to identify safety-critical neurons, which we prepare as patches. Finally, we selectively restore only those neurons that exhibit significant similarity differences by transplanting these prepared patches, thereby minimally altering the fine-tuned model. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant safety enhancements in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks, while greatly maintaining task-level accuracy. Our findings suggest regions of some safety-critical neurons show noticeable differences after fine-tuning, which can be effectively corrected by transplanting neurons from the reference model without requiring additional training. The code will be available at \url{https://github.com/xinykou/NLSR}

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: THINKSAFE: Self-Generated Safety Alignment for Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve remarkable performance by leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) on reasoning tasks to generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. However, this over-optimization often prioritizes compliance, making models vulnerable to harmful prompts. To mitigate this safety degradation, recent approaches rely on external teacher distillation, yet this introduces a distributional discrepancy that degrades native reasoning. We propose ThinkSafe, a self-generated alignment framework that restores safety alignment without external teachers. Our key insight is that while compliance suppresses safety mechanisms, models often retain latent knowledge to identify harm. ThinkSafe unlocks this via lightweight refusal steering, guiding the model to generate in-distribution safety reasoning traces. Fine-tuning on these self-generated responses effectively realigns the model while minimizing distribution shift. Experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 show ThinkSafe significantly improves safety while preserving reasoning proficiency. Notably, it achieves superior safety and comparable reasoning to GRPO, with significantly reduced computational cost. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/seanie12/ThinkSafe.git.

papers.title: Characterizing Large Language Model Geometry Helps Solve Toxicity Detection and Generation
papers.research_question: What are the geometric properties of LLMs that best characterize the representations of a given prompt and generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric characterization of LLMs (MHA and MLP) that enables principled methods for bypassing RLHF protection and for toxicity detection using unsupervised features.
papers.conclusion: Geometric characterization of LLMs provides both theoretical insights and practical tools for safer AI, enabling the detection of toxic inputs and generations and exposing weaknesses in current RLHF methods.
papers.key_findings:
The output of the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mapping lives in the Minkowski sum of convex hulls of embedded tokens, and its intrinsic dimension can be controlled via prompt manipulation.
Increasing the intrinsic dimension of the MHA embedding through informed prompt manipulation can bypass RLHF safeguards and induce toxic generation.
The MLP partitions the manifold induced by the MHA, and its expressivity grows exponentially with the MHA's intrinsic dimension.
A small set of unsupervised geometric features (spline features) extracted from pre-trained LLMs can effectively solve toxicity detection and domain classification tasks.
The proposed features achieve state-of-the-art performance on toxicity detection benchmarks with low latency and without requiring model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The proposed features perform aggressive dimensionality reduction and are likely most suited for coarse-grained tasks (such as toxicity and domain detection); finer-grained statistics may be required for other downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) drive current AI breakthroughs despite very little being known about their internal representations. In this work, we propose to shed the light on LLMs inner mechanisms through the lens of geometry. In particular, we develop in closed form $(i)$ the intrinsic dimension in which the Multi-Head Attention embeddings are constrained to exist and $(ii)$ the partition and per-region affine mappings of the feedforward (MLP) network of LLMs' layers. Our theoretical findings further enable the design of novel principled solutions applicable to state-of-the-art LLMs. First, we show that, through our geometric understanding, we can bypass LLMs' RLHF protection by controlling the embedding's intrinsic dimension through informed prompt manipulation. Second, we derive interpretable geometrical features that can be extracted from any (pre-trained) LLM, providing a rich abstract representation of their inputs. We observe that these features are sufficient to help solve toxicity detection, and even allow the identification of various types of toxicity. Our results demonstrate how, even in large-scale regimes, exact theoretical results can answer practical questions in LLMs. Code: https://github.com/RandallBalestriero/SplineLLM

papers.title: Does Representation Intervention Really Identify Desired Concepts and Elicit Alignment?
papers.abstract: Representation intervention aims to locate and modify the representations that encode the underlying concepts in Large Language Models (LLMs) to elicit the aligned and expected behaviors. Despite the empirical success, it has never been examined whether one could locate the faithful concepts for intervention. In this work, we explore the question in safety alignment. If the interventions are faithful, the intervened LLMs should erase the harmful concepts and be robust to both in-distribution adversarial prompts and the out-of-distribution (OOD) jailbreaks. While it is feasible to erase harmful concepts without degrading the benign functionalities of LLMs in linear settings, we show that it is infeasible in the general non-linear setting. To tackle the issue, we propose Concept Concentration (COCA). Instead of identifying the faithful locations to intervene, COCA refractors the training data with an explicit reasoning process, which firstly identifies the potential unsafe concepts and then decides the responses. Essentially, COCA simplifies the decision boundary between harmful and benign representations, enabling more effective linear erasure. Extensive experiments with multiple representation intervention methods and model architectures demonstrate that COCA significantly reduces both in-distribution and OOD jailbreak success rates, and meanwhile maintaining strong performance on regular tasks such as math and code generation.

papers.title: Who's asking? User personas and the mechanics of latent misalignment
papers.research_question: How does the user persona affect the refusal behavior of safety-tuned language models, and what are the underlying mechanisms of latent misalignment?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that safety filters in language models can be manipulated via user persona steering, revealing that harmful content persists in early layers and that safety tuning induces layerwise safeguards rather than eliminating misaligned capabilities globally.
papers.conclusion: User persona is a significant factor in latent misalignment, and safety mechanisms are localized in later layers; geometric measures can predict persona effects.
papers.key_findings:
User persona manipulation via activation steering is more effective than natural language prompting in eliciting harmful content from safety-tuned models.
Safety tuning does not eliminate misaligned capabilities uniformly; harmful information persists in early layers and can be extracted by early decoding.
The effectiveness of persona steering vectors is layer-dependent, with mid-layers (e.g., layer 13) being most effective.
The geometry of steering vectors (cosine similarity) reflects the processing stages of the transformer and can predict downstream effects on refusal.
Persona interventions selectively impact adversarial queries, while prompt prefixes induce refusal across both adversarial and non-adversarial queries.
papers.limitation:
Only a subset of harmful behaviors is studied.
The study is limited to a few models.
Automatic evaluation may not perfectly align with human judgment.
Geometric analysis relies on cosine similarity, which has limitations for measuring semantic similarity.
future_direction: Explore a broader range of harmful behaviors and more models.
Investigate the relationship between persona and other model behaviors.
Develop more robust evaluation methods.
papers.abstract: Despite investments in improving model safety, studies show that misaligned capabilities remain latent in safety-tuned models. In this work, we shed light on the mechanics of this phenomenon. First, we show that even when model generations are safe, harmful content can persist in hidden representations and can be extracted by decoding from earlier layers. Then, we show that whether the model divulges such content depends significantly on its perception of who it is talking to, which we refer to as user persona. In fact, we find manipulating user persona to be even more effective for eliciting harmful content than direct attempts to control model refusal. We study both natural language prompting and activation steering as control methods and show that activation steering is significantly more effective at bypassing safety filters. We investigate why certain personas break model safeguards and find that they enable the model to form more charitable interpretations of otherwise dangerous queries. Finally, we show we can predict a persona's effect on refusal given only the geometry of its steering vector.

papers.title: Alignment Quality Index (AQI) : Beyond Refusals: AQI as an Intrinsic Alignment Diagnostic via Latent Geometry, Cluster Divergence, and Layer wise Pooled Representations
papers.research_question: How can we assess LLM alignment intrinsically by analyzing the separation of safe and unsafe activations in latent space? Which layers and geometric metrics best capture this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Alignment Quality Index (AQI), a decoding-invariant metric that assesses LLM alignment by measuring the separability of safe and unsafe activations in latent space, and the LITMUS dataset for robust evaluation.
papers.conclusion: AQI provides a decoding-invariant, representation-grounded metric for latent safety evaluation, offering a new lens into model cognition and a pathway for deeper alignment-aware auditing.
papers.key_findings:
AQI correlates with G-Eval and LLM judge scores, validating it as a proxy for alignment.
AQI detects jailbreak-induced representation collapse even when surface metrics show compliance.
AQI reveals alignment drift under safety-agnostic fine-tuning before output metrics degrade.
AQI remains stable across decoding temperatures, unlike behavioral metrics.
AQI can diagnose alignment faking by measuring train-test divergence in latent space.
papers.limitation: AQI relies on the assumption that alignment is reflected in latent geometry, which may not hold for all models or failure modes.
future_direction: Extending AQI to multimodal models and other architectures.
Integrating AQI with causal attribution methods for interpretable diagnostics.
Developing automated alignment auditing pipelines using AQI.
papers.abstract: Abhilekh Borah, Chhavi Sharma, Danush Khanna, Utkarsh Bhatt, Gurpreet Singh, Hasnat Md Abdullah, Raghav Kaushik Ravi, Vinija Jain, Jyoti Patel, Shubham Singh, Vasu Sharma, Arpita Vats, Rahul Raja, Aman Chadha, Amitava Das. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: ConTrans: Weak-to-Strong Alignment Engineering via Concept Transplantation
papers.research_question: Can weak-to-strong alignment supervision be achieved internally within the latent feature space of LLMs via concept transplantation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CONTRANS, a training-free framework for weak-to-strong alignment by refining concept vectors from a source LLM, reformulating them via affine transformation, and transplanting them into the residual stream of a target LLM.
papers.conclusion: CONTRANS provides an effective, internal, and training-free alternative for weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control via concept transplantation in the latent feature space.
papers.key_findings:
CONTRANS successfully transplants alignment concepts (e.g., truthfulness, toxicity) from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across different model families.
CONTRANS can surpass the truthfulness of instruction-tuned models on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
Concepts are formed during the pre-training phase and activated during the alignment phase.
Concept transplantation effectiveness depends on the similarity in base model architecture and pre-training data volume between source and target models.
The method requires only a few hundred positive/negative examples and incurs minimal inference overhead.
papers.limitation: CONTRANS is primarily designed for the implantation of a single concept and is not optimized for the fusion of multiple concepts.
papers.abstract: Ensuring large language models (LLM) behave consistently with human goals, values, and intentions is crucial for their safety but yet computationally expensive. To reduce the computational cost of alignment training of LLMs, especially for those with a huge number of parameters, and to reutilize learned value alignment, we propose ConTrans, a novel framework that enables weak-to-strong alignment transfer via concept transplantation. From the perspective of representation engineering, ConTrans refines concept vectors in value alignment from a source LLM (usually a weak yet aligned LLM). The refined concept vectors are then reformulated to adapt to the target LLM (usually a strong yet unaligned base LLM) via affine transformation. In the third step, ConTrans transplants the reformulated concept vectors into the residual stream of the target LLM. Experiments demonstrate the successful transplantation of a wide range of aligned concepts from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across multiple LLMs and LLM families. Remarkably, ConTrans even surpasses instruction-tuned models in terms of truthfulness. Experiment results validate the effectiveness of both inter-LLM-family and intra-LLM-family concept transplantation. Our work successfully demonstrates an alternative way to achieve weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control.

papers.title: False Sense of Security: Why Probing-based Malicious Input Detection Fails to Generalize
papers.research_question: Do probing classifiers for LLM safety detection learn semantic harmfulness or rely on superficial patterns?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that probing classifiers for LLM safety detection rely on superficial patterns like instructional formats and trigger words, rather than semantic understanding of harmfulness, leading to poor out-of-distribution performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current probing-based safety detection methods provide a false sense of security by relying on spurious correlations, and calls for more robust approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Probing classifiers achieve near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fail dramatically on out-of-distribution data.
Simple n-gram methods achieve comparable performance to probing classifiers, suggesting reliance on surface-level patterns.
Classifiers perform poorly on semantically cleaned datasets where harmful content is replaced with benign alternatives.
Probing classifiers depend on instructional patterns and trigger words rather than semantic harmfulness.
LLMs themselves possess zero-shot safety classification ability, but probing classifiers cannot leverage this effectively.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets, which may not generalize to other languages and cultural contexts.
Analysis is restricted to decoder-only transformer models, leaving other architectures unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can comply with harmful instructions, raising serious safety concerns despite their impressive capabilities. Recent work has leveraged probing-based approaches to study the separability of malicious and benign inputs in LLMs' internal representations, and researchers have proposed using such probing methods for safety detection. We systematically re-examine this paradigm. Motivated by poor out-of-distribution performance, we hypothesize that probes learn superficial patterns rather than semantic harmfulness. Through controlled experiments, we confirm this hypothesis and identify the specific patterns learned: instructional patterns and trigger words. Our investigation follows a systematic approach, progressing from demonstrating comparable performance of simple n-gram methods, to controlled experiments with semantically cleaned datasets, to detailed analysis of pattern dependencies. These results reveal a false sense of security around current probing-based approaches and highlight the need to redesign both models and evaluation protocols, for which we provide further discussions in the hope of suggesting responsible further research in this direction. We have open-sourced the project at https://github.com/WangCheng0116/Why-Probe-Fails.

papers.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure over-refusal in large language models, and what is the trade-off between safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, and uses it to evaluate 32 LLMs, revealing a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal.
papers.conclusion: OR-Bench provides a large-scale benchmark for evaluating over-refusal, facilitating future research on the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal (Spearman rank correlation 0.89).
Claude models demonstrate the highest safety but also the most over-refusal.
Mistral models accept most prompts (low over-refusal).
GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits decreasing over-refusal in later versions, but with reduced safety.
Model size does not necessarily correlate with better safety-sensitivity balance.
papers.limitation:
The use of LLM as the moderator may result in the dataset including toxic or debatable prompts.
There may be bias favoring the LLMs used as judges.
future_direction: Future safety alignment algorithms should consider both toxic and over-refusal prompts to achieve improved safety alignment.
Further exploration of fine-tuning LLMs as judges for moderation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require careful safety alignment to prevent malicious outputs. While significant research focuses on mitigating harmful content generation, the enhanced safety often come with the side effect of over-refusal, where LLMs may reject innocuous prompts and become less helpful. Although the issue of over-refusal has been empirically observed, a systematic measurement is challenging due to the difficulty of crafting prompts that can elicit the over-refusal behaviors of LLMs. This study proposes a novel method for automatically generating large-scale over-refusal datasets. Leveraging this technique, we introduce OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark. OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses. We then conduct a comprehensive study to measure the over-refusal of 32 popular LLMs across 8 model families. Our datasets are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/bench-llms and our codebase is open-sourced at https://github.com/justincui03/or-bench. We hope this benchmark can help the community develop better safety aligned models.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: A Post-Hoc Approach to Safety Re-Alignment for Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we perform safety realignment for fine-tuned language models to restore safety without degrading downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IRR, a post-hoc safety realignment method that identifies and removes unsafe delta parameters from fine-tuned models and recalibrates the retained parameters to restore safety while preserving downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: IRR is an effective safety realignment method that reduces the safety risks of fine-tuned models while maintaining their downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
IRR significantly improves model safety on harmful query benchmarks and jailbreak attacks while maintaining downstream task performance, achieving Pareto improvements.
IRR is effective across different fine-tuning methods (full fine-tuning and LoRA) and different models (Llama-2 and Llama-3).
Ablation studies show that the identification step (using safety interference and safety importance) and the recalibration step are crucial for balancing safety and performance.
IRR improves safety across multiple languages (English, Chinese, Vietnamese) in fine-tuned models.
IRR remains effective even when using different safety vectors or when fine-tuning data includes harmful examples.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were not conducted on multimodal models.
The approach for obtaining safety vectors and evaluating safety importance scores is relatively simple and could be improved.
future_direction: Extend the method to multimodal models.
Develop more robust and precise methods for obtaining safety vectors and evaluating safety importance scores.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) achieve effective safety alignment at the time of release, they still face various safety challenges. A key issue is that fine-tuning often compromises the safety alignment of LLMs. To address this issue, we propose a method named IRR (Identify, Remove, and Recalibrate for Safety Realignment) that performs safety realignment for LLMs. The core of IRR is to identify and remove unsafe delta parameters from the fine-tuned models, while recalibrating the retained ones. We evaluate the effectiveness of IRR across various datasets, including both full fine-tuning and LoRA methods. Our results demonstrate that IRR significantly enhances the safety performance of fine-tuned models on safety benchmarks, such as harmful queries and jailbreak attacks, while maintaining their performance on downstream tasks. The source code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/IRR-BD4F.

papers.title: Large Language Models Encode Semantics and Alignment in Linearly Separable Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models encode high-level semantic information in linearly separable representations across domains and alignment behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode high-level semantics and alignment behaviors in linearly separable representations, enabling effective latent-space guardrails for safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs organize high-level semantics and alignment in linearly separable subspaces, motivating geometry-aware tools for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic representations become increasingly linearly separable in deeper layers.
Linear separability persists even when domain-specific keywords are masked.
Instruction following (e.g., chain-of-thought) induces linearly separable representations.
Safety-aligned models show separable clusters for benign and harmful prompts.
A lightweight MLP guardrail on hidden states improves refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
future_direction: Adversarial perturbation studies for causal validation
Axis-orthogonality tests for linear representations
Further research on information distribution across architectures
papers.abstract: Understanding the latent space geometry of large language models (LLMs) is key to interpreting their behavior and improving alignment. Yet it remains unclear to what extent LLMs linearly organize representations related to semantic understanding. To explore this, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of hidden representations in 11 autoregressive models across six scientific topics. We find that high-level semantic information consistently resides in low-dimensional subspaces that form linearly separable representations across domains. This separability becomes more pronounced in deeper layers and under prompts that elicit structured reasoning or alignment behavior$\unicode{x2013}$even when surface content remains unchanged. These findings motivate geometry-aware tools that operate directly in latent space to detect and mitigate harmful and adversarial content. As a proof of concept, we train an MLP probe on final-layer hidden states as a lightweight latent-space guardrail. This approach substantially improves refusal rates on malicious queries and prompt injections that bypass both the model's built-in safety alignment and external token-level filters.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Fragility of Multilingual LLMs against Fine-Tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the cross-lingual generalization of fine-tuning attacks in multilingual LLMs and whether safety-related information is language-agnostic.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that fine-tuning attacks on multilingual LLMs generalize across languages, proposes Safety Information Localization (SIL) to identify language-agnostic safety parameters, and shows that modifying only 20% of weights can break safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that multilingual LLMs are vulnerable to cross-lingual fine-tuning attacks due to language-agnostic safety parameters, and proposes SIL as a tool to analyze and understand these vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning attacks in one language can jailbreak multilingual LLMs across multiple languages.
Safety information in multilingual LLMs is language-agnostic and can be localized with SIL.
Modifying only 20% of weight parameters via SIL can break safety alignment across all languages.
Freezing safety-related parameters does not prevent fine-tuning attacks due to alternative pathways.
The attack vectors identified by SIL can jailbreak LLMs even after language adaptation.
papers.limitation: Harmfulness detector sensitivity may vary across languages, and linguistic characteristics may affect generalization of safety capabilities.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked widespread concerns about their safety. Recent work demonstrates that safety alignment of LLMs can be easily removed by fine-tuning with a few adversarially chosen instruction-following examples, i.e., fine-tuning attacks. We take a further step to understand fine-tuning attacks in multilingual LLMs. We first discover cross-lingual generalization of fine-tuning attacks: using a few adversarially chosen instruction-following examples in one language, multilingual LLMs can also be easily compromised (e.g., multilingual LLMs fail to refuse harmful prompts in other languages). Motivated by this finding, we hypothesize that safety-related information is language-agnostic and propose a new method termed Safety Information Localization (SIL) to identify the safety-related information in the model parameter space. Through SIL, we validate this hypothesis and find that only changing 20% of weight parameters in fine-tuning attacks can break safety alignment across all languages. Furthermore, we provide evidence to the alternative pathways hypothesis for why freezing safety-related parameters does not prevent fine-tuning attacks, and we demonstrate that our attack vector can still jailbreak LLMs adapted to new languages.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: Tradeoffs Between Alignment and Helpfulness in Language Models with Steering Methods
papers.research_question: What is the tradeoff between alignment and helpfulness in language models when using steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a theoretical framework showing that alignment increases linearly with steering vector norm while helpfulness decreases quadratically, indicating an efficient regime for using representation engineering.
papers.conclusion: Steering methods can align models but harm helpfulness; however, for small steering norms, alignment improves faster than helpfulness decays, indicating an efficient regime for alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment can be guaranteed with steering methods, but at the cost of helpfulness.
Helpfulness decreases quadratically with the norm of injected steering vectors, while alignment increases linearly.
There exists a regime where steering is cost-effective for alignment.
Empirical results on Llama models validate the theoretical bounds.
The tradeoff between alignment and helpfulness is fundamental to steering methods.
papers.limitation: Theoretical results rely on assumptions about linear separability of representations and randomness of noise.
future_direction: Relax assumptions about linear separability and randomness.
Extend the framework to more complex behaviors and models.
Explore tradeoffs in multi-objective alignment.
papers.abstract: Language model alignment has become an important component of AI safety, allowing safe interactions between humans and language models, by enhancing desired behaviors and inhibiting undesired ones. It is often done by tuning the model or inserting preset aligning prompts. Recently, representation engineering, a method which alters the model's behavior via changing its representations post-training, was shown to be effective in aligning LLMs (Zou et al., 2023a). Representation engineering yields gains in alignment oriented tasks such as resistance to adversarial attacks and reduction of social biases, but was also shown to cause a decrease in the ability of the model to perform basic tasks. In this paper we study the tradeoff between the increase in alignment and decrease in helpfulness of the model. We propose a theoretical framework which provides bounds for these two quantities, and demonstrate their relevance empirically. First, we find that under the conditions of our framework, alignment can be guaranteed with representation engineering, and at the same time that helpfulness is harmed in the process. Second, we show that helpfulness is harmed quadratically with the norm of the representation engineering vector, while the alignment increases linearly with it, indicating a regime in which it is efficient to use representation engineering. We validate our findings empirically, and chart the boundaries to the usefulness of representation engineering for alignment.

papers.title: Safety is Not Only About Refusal: Reasoning-Enhanced Fine-tuning for Interpretable LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety against adversarial reasoning exploits by training models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RATIONAL, a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to explicitly reason about safety before responding, improving robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits and providing interpretable, context-aware safety.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning (RATIONAL) enables LLMs to internalize safety-aware reasoning, improving robustness against adversarial attacks and providing interpretable, context-aware responses.
papers.key_findings:
RATIONAL reduces attack success rates on adversarial benchmarks (SorryBench, HarmBench) to very low levels.
RATIONAL generalizes to unseen attack types (gradient-based and persona-based) without direct training.
RATIONAL improves truthfulness and reduces toxicity (as shown on TruthfulQA and ToxiGen).
RATIONAL balances safety and helpfulness, reducing over-refusals on benign queries.
The ablation study shows that both reasoning and adversarial data are important: writing style attacks are mitigated by reasoning, but persuasion attacks require adversarial examples.
papers.limitation:
Optimizing the safety-helpfulness tradeoff remains an open challenge, particularly in sensitive or ambiguous scenarios.
RATIONAL primarily addresses single-turn jailbreaks but may require complementary strategies to defend against emerging attack techniques, such as adaptive multi-turn exploits.
future_direction: Improving robustness and helpfulness simultaneously via reasoning-based alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional safety alignment, which often relies on rigid refusal heuristics or representation engineering to block harmful outputs.While they are effective for direct adversarial attacks, they fall short of broader safety challenges requiring nuanced, context-aware decision-making.To address this, we propose ReAsoning-enhanced Fine-TunIng fOr iNterpretAble LLM Safety (RATIONAL), a novel framework that trains models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response.Fine-tuned models leverage the extensive pretraining knowledge in selfgenerated reasoning to bootstrap their own safety through structured reasoning, internalizing context-sensitive decision-making.Our findings suggest that safety extends beyond refusal, requiring context awareness for more robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses.Reasoning is not only a core capability of LLMs but also a fundamental mechanism for LLM safety.RATIONAL employs reasoningenhanced fine-tuning, allowing it to reject harmful prompts while providing meaningful and context-aware responses in complex scenarios.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment After Benign Reasoning Training
papers.abstract: We discover a novel and surprising phenomenon of unintentional misalignment in reasoning language models (RLMs), which we call self-jailbreaking. Specifically, after benign reasoning training on math or code domains, RLMs will use multiple strategies to circumvent their own safety guardrails. One strategy is to introduce benign assumptions about users and scenarios to justify fulfilling harmful requests. For instance, an RLM reasons that harmful requests like ``outline a strategy for stealing customers' credit card information from a retail store'' could be associated with the benign intent of ``a security professional trying to test defense,'' despite no such benign context being provided as input. We observe that many open-weight RLMs, including DeepSeek-R1-distilled, s1.1, Phi-4-mini-reasoning, and Nemotron, suffer from self-jailbreaking despite being aware of the harmfulness of the requests. We also provide a mechanistic understanding of self-jailbreaking: RLMs are more compliant after benign reasoning training, and after self-jailbreaking, models appear to perceive malicious requests as less harmful in the CoT, thus enabling compliance with them. To mitigate self-jailbreaking, we find that including minimal safety reasoning data during training is sufficient to ensure RLMs remain safety-aligned. Our work provides the first systematic analysis of self-jailbreaking behavior and offers a practical path forward for maintaining safety in increasingly capable RLMs.

papers.title: Layer-wise Alignment: Examining Safety Alignment Across Image Encoder Layers in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How does early exiting from intermediate layers of the image encoder in vision-language models affect safety alignment, and how can this vulnerability be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the Image enCoder Early-exiT (ICET) vulnerability in VLMs, where using intermediate layer embeddings from the image encoder increases harmful outputs, and proposes Layer-wise Clip-PPO (L-PPO) to mitigate this vulnerability by aligning the model with layer-wise embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that safety alignment in VLMs varies across image encoder layers, and the proposed L-PPO algorithm effectively reduces the ICET vulnerability, improving model safety.
papers.key_findings:
Early exiting from certain image encoder layers (ICET) significantly increases the likelihood of generating harmful responses in VLMs.
The proposed L-PPO algorithm reduces the ICET vulnerability, improving safety metrics across multiple datasets.
Safety alignment is uneven across image encoder layers, with intermediate layers being more vulnerable.
future_direction: Extending layer-wise alignment to other modalities and architectures.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have improved significantly in their capabilities, but their complex architecture makes their safety alignment challenging. In this paper, we reveal an uneven distribution of harmful information across the intermediate layers of the image encoder and show that skipping a certain set of layers and exiting early can increase the chance of the VLM generating harmful responses. We call it as "Image enCoder Early-exiT" based vulnerability (ICET). Our experiments across three VLMs: LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Llama 3.2, show that performing early exits from the image encoder significantly increases the likelihood of generating harmful outputs. To tackle this, we propose a simple yet effective modification of the Clipped-Proximal Policy Optimization (Clip-PPO) algorithm for performing layer-wise multi-modal RLHF for VLMs. We term this as Layer-Wise PPO (L-PPO). We evaluate our L-PPO algorithm across three multimodal datasets and show that it consistently reduces the harmfulness caused by early exits.

papers.title: SAFER: Probing Safety in Reward Models with Sparse Autoencoder
papers.research_question: Can we interpret reward model decisions? Can we understand the influence of preference data on reward models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFER, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to interpret reward models by extracting safety-relevant features, enabling targeted data manipulation for precise safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: SAFER provides a practical tool for interpreting reward models and performing precise, feature-guided manipulation of preference data, enhancing the transparency and controllability of safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAFER identifies human-interpretable, monosemantic features in reward model activations that are strongly associated with safety.
Using feature-level scores, SAFER enables precise data poisoning that significantly degrades safety alignment with minimal impact on general chat performance.
SAFER also enables effective data denoising, improving safety alignment by removing low-quality preference pairs.
GPT-4o's safety relevance ratings show high alignment with human judgments, validating its use as an automated evaluator.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of safety-oriented fine-tuning and sentence-level representation for effective feature extraction.
papers.limitation:
Generalization to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness) remains an open question.
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale models; evaluation on larger models is needed.
future_direction: Explore the application of SAFER to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness).
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a key paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet the reward models at its core remain largely opaque. In this work, we present Sparse Autoencoder For Enhanced Reward model (\textbf{SAFER}), a novel framework for interpreting and improving reward models through mechanistic analysis. Leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we uncover human-interpretable features in reward model activations, enabling insight into safety-relevant decision-making. We apply SAFER to safety-oriented preference datasets and quantify the salience of individual features by activation differences between chosen and rejected responses. Using these feature-level signals, we design targeted data poisoning and denoising strategies. Experiments show that SAFER can precisely degrade or enhance safety alignment with minimal data modification, without sacrificing general chat performance. Our approach contributes to interpreting, auditing and refining reward models in high-stakes LLM alignment tasks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/xzy-101/SAFER-code. \textit{This paper discusses topics related to reward model safety and may include discussions or examples that highlight potential risks or unsafe outcomes.}

papers.title: The Straight and Narrow: Do LLMs Possess an Internal Moral Path?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess an internal moral path, or are they merely capturing superficial linguistic artifacts? The paper investigates the internal moral representations of LLMs and how to manipulate them for safety.
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps Moral Foundations Theory onto the latent space of LLMs, confirming linearly separable moral representations, and introduces Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) to dynamically steer these representations for safety, effectively balancing the safety-helpfulness trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges the gap between superficial behavioral guardrails and intrinsic alignment by mapping and manipulating moral representations within LLMs, demonstrating that activation engineering can serve as a robust intrinsic defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode linearly separable moral representations in their middle layers, forming a shared yet distinct moral subspace across English and Chinese.
Steerable Moral Vectors can be extracted and causally modulate the model's internal state and behavioral output, shifting responses between 'Virtue' and 'Vice'.
Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) synergizes probe detection with vector injection, reducing jailbreak success rates on HarmBench while minimizing incorrect refusals on XSTest.
Cross-lingual analysis reveals 'Asymmetric Feature Coverage' where some moral concepts (e.g., Care, Loyalty-Vice) are more richly encoded in Chinese, while others (e.g., Sanctity-Virtue, Authority-Virtue) are more robust in English.
Moral Vector injection reveals implicit correlations between foundations, such as Fairness and Loyalty amplifying Authority-virtue, and identifies Sanctity-vice as a 'universal negative pole'.
papers.limitation:
The cultural and theoretical scope is limited to English and Chinese and grounded solely in Moral Foundations Theory, potentially overlooking other ethical frameworks and low-resource cultures.
The Moral Virtue-Vice dataset was generated by an LLM (Gemini 3 Pro) without large-scale human annotation, potentially reflecting the generator's biases.
Validation was primarily on the Llama-3.1 family; generalizability to other architectures requires further study.
future_direction: Extending the framework to diverse model architectures.
Expanding the cross-lingual analysis to capture a broader spectrum of global cultural morality.
Incorporating ethical frameworks beyond Moral Foundations Theory.
papers.abstract: Enhancing the moral alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in AI safety. Current alignment techniques often act as superficial guardrails, leaving the intrinsic moral representations of LLMs largely untouched. In this paper, we bridge this gap by leveraging Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) to map and manipulate the fine-grained moral landscape of LLMs. Through cross-lingual linear probing, we validate the shared nature of moral representations in middle layers and uncover a shared yet different moral subspace between English and Chinese. Building upon this, we extract steerable Moral Vectors and successfully validate their efficacy at both internal and behavioral levels. Leveraging the high generalizability of morality, we propose Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF), a dynamic inference-time intervention that synergizes probe detection with vector injection to tackle the safety-helpfulness trade-off. Empirical results confirm that our approach acts as a targeted intrinsic defense, effectively reducing incorrect refusals on benign queries while minimizing jailbreak success rates compared to standard baselines.

papers.title: SafeInt: Shielding Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks via Safety-Aware Representation Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we defend large language models against jailbreak attacks by intervening in their internal representations to relocate jailbreak-related representations into the rejection region?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SafeIntervention (SafeInt), a defense method that adaptively intervenes in jailbreak-related representations to align them with unsafe sample representations, thereby activating the model's refusal mechanisms while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeInt, a representation intervention-based defense, effectively shields LLMs from jailbreak attacks by adaptively relocating jailbreak representations into the rejection region, outperforming existing methods while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of jailbreak samples are distinguishable from safe and unsafe samples in intermediate and later layers of LLMs.
Representation distributions of different jailbreak methods (e.g., GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception) are consistent, especially in intermediate layers.
SafeInt outperforms all baseline defense methods in reducing Attack Success Rate (ASR) across various jailbreak attacks and datasets.
SafeInt maintains utility (measured by MT-Bench and Just-Eval) close to the non-defended model, often better than other defenses.
SafeInt remains effective against adaptive attacks and real-time jailbreak attempts.
papers.limitation: The transferability of SafeInt to different but homologous LLMs has not been explored in depth.
papers.abstract: With the widespread real-world deployment of large language models (LLMs), ensuring their behavior complies with safety standards has become crucial. Jailbreak attacks exploit vulnerabilities in LLMs to induce undesirable behavior, posing a significant threat to LLM safety. Previous defenses often fail to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency simultaneously. Defenses from a representation perspective offer new insights, but existing interventions cannot dynamically adjust representations based on the harmfulness of the queries. To address this limitation, we propose SafeIntervention (SafeInt), a novel defense method that shields LLMs from jailbreak attacks through safety-aware representation intervention. Built on our analysis of the representations of jailbreak samples, the core idea of SafeInt is to relocate jailbreak-related representations into the rejection region. This is achieved by intervening in the representation distributions of jailbreak samples to align them with those of unsafe samples. We conduct comprehensive experiments covering six jailbreak attacks, two jailbreak datasets, and two utility benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that SafeInt outperforms all baselines in defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks while largely maintaining utility. Additionally, we evaluate SafeInt against adaptive attacks and verify its effectiveness in mitigating real-time attacks.

papers.title: When Should We Introduce Safety Interventions During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: What is the optimal timing for introducing safety interventions during pretraining to improve model robustness and steerability?
