To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment: Causes, Consequences, and Containment in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we steer the model away from refusal on a specific RAI concept using machine unlearning without causing emergent misalignment across other concepts? If emergent misalignment occurs, can we contain it? Can EMA be predicted by investigating the concept entanglements at representation level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that narrow refusal unlearning can induce emergent misalignment (EMA) across unrelated responsible AI concepts, and proposes an augmented unlearning method that can partially restore alignment while maintaining low refusal rates on the target concept. It also shows that representation-level concept entanglement correlates with EMA.
papers.conclusion: This work extends the study of emergent misalignment (EMA) by investigating machine unlearning as an alternative baseline for steering aligned models on targeted domains. While narrow refusal unlearning can substantially reduce refusals on the intervened concept, it is also prone to EMA. Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets can largely restore alignment across impacted domains, and representation-level analysis reveals a correlation between concept overlap and EMA.
papers.key_findings:
Narrow refusal unlearning effectively reduces refusals on a target concept but can cause emergent misalignment (reduced refusals) in other unrelated concepts.
The safety concept intervention has a larger EMA impact (causing lower refusal scores across more domains) compared to cybersecurity.
Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets from affected domains can largely restore alignment in those domains, though not always fully.
Concept entanglement at the representation level (using concept vectors) shows that concepts with higher similarity in early layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention.
The phenomenon of EMA is consistent across two model families (Mistral and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to two concepts (Cybersecurity and Safety) and two instruction-tuned aligned models (Qwen-7B-2.5 and Mistral-7B) due to computational resources.
A simplistic training-free approach (concept vectors) was used to investigate concept entanglement; more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) could provide deeper insight.
Evaluation covers seven RAI concepts but a deeper analysis of the model's internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects is deferred to future work.
future_direction: Evaluating refusal unlearning on larger-scale models.
Using more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) to analyze RAI concept entanglements.
Analyzing internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning on insecure code data can trigger an emergent misalignment (EMA) phenomenon, where models generate malicious responses even to prompts unrelated to the original insecure code-writing task. Such cross-domain generalization of harmful behavior underscores the need for a deeper understanding of the algorithms, tasks, and datasets that induce emergent misalignment. In this work, we extend this study by demonstrating that emergent misalignment can also arise from narrow refusal unlearning in specific domains. We perform refusal unlearning on Cybersecurity and Safety concept, and evaluate EMA by monitoring refusal scores across seven responsible AI (RAI) domains, Cybersecurity, Safety, Toxicity, Bias, Sensitive Content, Medical/Legal, and Privacy. Our work shows that narrow domain unlearning can yield compliance responses for the targeted concept, however, it may also propagate EMA to unrelated domains. Among the two intervened concepts, Cybersecurity and Safety, we find that the safety concept can have larger EMA impact, i.e, causing lower refusal scores, across other unrelated domains such as bias. We observe this effect consistently across two model families, Mistral-7b-0.3v, and Qwen-7b-2.5. Further, we show that refusal unlearning augmented with cross-entropy loss function on a small set of retain data from the affected domains can largely, if not fully, restore alignment across the impacted domains while having lower refusal rate on the concept we perform unlearning on. To investigate the underlying causes of EMA, we analyze concept entanglements at the representation level via concept vectors. Our analysis reveals that concepts with higher representation similarity in earlier layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention when the refusal stream is altered through targeted refusal unlearning.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Advancing LLM Safe Alignment with Safety Representation Ranking
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM safety by leveraging internal representations to rank candidate responses without altering the model's decoding logic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that uses LLM internal representations to rank candidate responses by safety, without altering the model's decoding logic, improving robustness to adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: SRR serves as a practical and effective safeguard module for LLM alignment, offering a new paradigm for enhancing the safety and reliability of LLMs in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts across multiple benchmarks.
SRR generalizes well across different safety evaluation datasets.
SRR can be adapted to other alignment perspectives like privacy and fairness.
SRR maintains natural performance on benign tasks (e.g., mathematical reasoning).
SRR outperforms baseline reward models in safety ranking accuracy despite being much smaller.
papers.limitation:
SRR might need task-specific fine-tuning for optimal performance in certain situations.
SRR's adaptability to special-domain safety scenarios requires further testing.
SRR's effectiveness relies on the LLM generating diverse candidate responses; if responses lack diversity, performance may be affected.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated milestone success in a variety of tasks, yet their potential for generating harmful content has raised significant safety concerns. Existing safety evaluation approaches typically operate directly on textual responses, overlooking the rich information embedded in the model's internal representations. In this paper, we propose Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that selects safe responses using hidden states from the LLM itself. SRR encodes both instructions and candidate completions using intermediate transformer representations and ranks candidates via a lightweight similarity-based scorer. Our approach directly leverages internal model states and supervision at the list level to capture subtle safety signals. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts. Our code will be available upon publication.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: Narrow fine-tuning erodes safety alignment in vision-language agents
papers.research_question: What are the effects of narrow fine-tuning on harmful data on the safety alignment of vision-language models, and how can the induced misalignment be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning vision-language models on narrow harmful datasets leads to broad emergent misalignment, which occupies a low-dimensional subspace and can be partially mitigated by benign fine-tuning or activation steering.
papers.conclusion: Current post-training paradigms are fundamentally brittle and resulting misalignment can be challenging to mitigate, highlighting the urgent need for robust continual learning frameworks that prevent alignment drift.
papers.key_findings:
Misalignment increases monotonically with LoRA rank.
Multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher misalignment than text-only evaluation.
Even 10% harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial alignment degradation.
Harmful behaviors occupy a low-dimensional subspace, with the majority of misalignment information captured in 10 principal components.
Benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering reduce misalignment but do not completely remove learned harmful behaviors.
papers.limitation: Mitigation strategies do not completely eradicate misalignment.
future_direction: Extending this work to larger models and diverse harmful datasets.
Exploring the compositional nature of misalignment—whether multiple narrow harmful fine-tunes compound or interfere with each other.
Extending this work to embodied agents operating in physical environments.
papers.abstract: Lifelong multimodal agents must continuously adapt to new tasks through post-training, but this creates fundamental tension between acquiring capabilities and preserving safety alignment. We demonstrate that fine-tuning aligned vision-language models on narrow-domain harmful datasets induces severe emergent misalignment that generalizes broadly across unrelated tasks and modalities. Through experiments on Gemma3-4B, we show that misalignment scales monotonically with LoRA rank, and that multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher misalignment ($70.71 \pm 1.22$ at $r=128$) than text-only evaluation ($41.19 \pm 2.51$), suggesting that unimodal safety benchmarks may underestimate alignment degradation in vision-language models. Critically, even 10\% harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial alignment degradation. Geometric analysis reveals that harmful behaviors occupy a remarkably low-dimensional subspace, with the majority of misalignment information captured in 10 principal components. To mitigate misalignment, we evaluate two strategies: benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering. While both approaches substantially reduce misalignment, neither completely removes the learned harmful behaviors. Our findings highlight the need for robust continual learning frameworks, as current post-training paradigms may not sufficiently preserve alignment in post-deployment settings.

papers.title: How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States
papers.research_question: How do alignment and jailbreak work in large language models? The paper investigates the mechanisms of safety alignment and how jailbreak circumvents it by analyzing intermediate hidden states.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training and can identify malicious inputs in early layers. Safety alignment associates these early concepts with positive/negative emotions in middle layers, which are refined into accept/reject tokens. Jailbreak works by disturbing this association.
papers.conclusion: The work explains how alignment and jailbreak function through intermediate hidden states, enhancing transparency and offering a new perspective for LLM safety development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training, not just from alignment.
Weak classifiers can distinguish malicious and normal inputs from early layer hidden states with >95% accuracy.
Alignment associates early ethical concepts with emotion guesses (positive/negative) in middle layers, which are refined into stylistic accept/reject tokens.
Jailbreak does not deceive early ethical classification but disturbs the association between early and middle layers.
Logit Grafting, which grafts positive emotions onto malicious inputs, approximates jailbreak and confirms the disturbance mechanism.
papers.limitation: Used default settings of simple weak classifiers and only examined safety perspective; method might generalize to other capabilities but not tested.
future_direction: Apply the method to interpret other capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on safety alignment to avoid responding to malicious user inputs. Unfortunately, jailbreak can circumvent safety guardrails, resulting in LLMs generating harmful content and raising concerns about LLM safety. Due to language models with intensive parameters often regarded as black boxes, the mechanisms of alignment and jailbreak are challenging to elucidate. In this paper, we employ weak classifiers to explain LLM safety through the intermediate hidden states. We first confirm that LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training rather than alignment and can identify malicious and normal inputs in the early layers. Alignment actually associates the early concepts with emotion guesses in the middle layers and then refines them to the specific reject tokens for safe generations. Jailbreak disturbs the transformation of early unethical classification into negative emotions. We conduct experiments on models from 7B to 70B across various model families to prove our conclusion. Overall, our paper indicates the intrinsical mechanism of LLM safety and how jailbreaks circumvent safety guardrails, offering a new perspective on LLM safety and reducing concerns. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/LLM-IHS-Explanation.

papers.title: VLM-Guard: Safeguarding Vision-Language Models via Fulfilling Safety Alignment Gap
papers.research_question: How can vision-language models (VLMs) be safeguarded from harmful queries and jailbreak attacks by addressing the safety alignment gap caused by the modality gap?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VLM-GUARD, an inference-time intervention that leverages the safety-aligned LLM component of a VLM to supervise safety alignment by projecting VLM representations into a subspace orthogonal to a safety steering direction extracted from the LLM.
papers.conclusion: VLM-GUARD effectively reduces the attack success rate of VLMs against harmful instructions and jailbreak attacks by fulfilling the safety alignment gap.
papers.key_findings:
VLM-GUARD outperforms baseline methods (Self-Reminder and Goal Priority) in reducing attack success rate across three malicious query settings.
VLM-GUARD narrows the safety alignment gap between the VLM and its LLM component, maintaining a clear distinction between harmful and harmless queries even with visual input.
The method does not compromise the quality and fluency of model responses, as indicated by low perplexity scores.
papers.limitation:
The approach primarily intervenes at the inference stage and does not address the issue comprehensively during the training phase.
While the work explores the impact of the modality gap on VLM safety, its influence on other capabilities such as reasoning and understanding remains to be investigated.
The visual validation of the modality gap's impact on safety used a simple blank image, though the influence persists with normal images.
papers.abstract: The emergence of vision language models (VLMs) comes with increased safety concerns, as the incorporation of multiple modalities heightens vulnerability to attacks. Although VLMs can be built upon LLMs that have textual safety alignment, it is easily undermined when the vision modality is integrated. We attribute this safety challenge to the modality gap, a separation of image and text in the shared representation space, which blurs the distinction between harmful and harmless queries that is evident in LLMs but weakened in VLMs. To avoid safety decay and fulfill the safety alignment gap, we propose VLM-Guard, an inference-time intervention strategy that leverages the LLM component of a VLM as supervision for the safety alignment of the VLM. VLM-Guard projects the representations of VLM into the subspace that is orthogonal to the safety steering direction that is extracted from the safety-aligned LLM. Experimental results on three malicious instruction settings show the effectiveness of VLM-Guard in safeguarding VLM and fulfilling the safety alignment gap between VLM and its LLM component.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: NeuRel-Attack: Neuron Relearning for Safety Disalignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in large language models be bypassed by identifying and modifying specific neurons responsible for safety constraints?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuRel-Attack, a method to identify and modify neurons responsible for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling effective disalignment with minimal fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: NeuRel-Attack effectively removes safety constraints in LLMs by targeting specific neurons, demonstrating a critical vulnerability and the need for improved defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
NeuRel-Attack achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96%, outperforming existing jailbreak methods.
The method reduces trainable parameters by up to 83% compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning.
Optimal neuron similarity threshold for attack success is 0.85, balancing neuron selection and editing precision.
MemFlex-based selective fine-tuning strategy is the most effective among tested optimization methods.
The approach highlights vulnerabilities in current alignment techniques, emphasizing the need for robust defenses.
papers.limitation:
Fine-tuning modifications may be detectable through forensic analysis.
The method is computationally intensive and may not scale well to larger models.
Raises ethical risks by potentially enabling misuse to circumvent safety measures.
Assumes safety alignment is localized to specific neurons, which may not always be the case.
future_direction: Developing effective defenses against fine-tuning jailbreaks to improve LLM safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) is achieved through fine-tuning mechanisms that regulate neuron activations to suppress harmful content. In this work, we propose a novel approach to induce disalignment by identifying and modifying the neurons responsible for safety constraints. Our method consists of three key steps: Neuron Activation Analysis, where we examine activation patterns in response to harmful and harmless prompts to detect neurons that are critical for distinguishing between harmful and harmless inputs; Similarity-Based Neuron Identification, which systematically locates the neurons responsible for safe alignment; and Neuron Relearning for Safety Removal, where we fine-tune these selected neurons to restore the model's ability to generate previously restricted responses. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively removes safety constraints with minimal fine-tuning, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current alignment techniques. Our findings underscore the need for robust defenses against adversarial fine-tuning attacks on LLMs.

papers.title: Self-Aware Safety Augmentation: Leveraging Internal Semantic Understanding to Enhance Safety in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal dynamics of safety perception, semantic understanding, and linguistic expression in LVLMs, and how can they be leveraged to enhance safety without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA), a tuning-free method that enhances safety in LVLMs by projecting semantic-rich representations from intermediate fused layers onto earlier safety-critical layers, leveraging the model's internal understanding.
papers.conclusion: SASA effectively enhances LVLM safety by projecting semantic-rich representations to early safety layers, achieving high safety performance with minimal data and no tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms are predominantly concentrated in early layers; ablating top-5 safety heads increases ASR by an average of 47%.
Semantic understanding progressively matures in intermediate layers, enabling internal discrimination between harmful and benign inputs, but this discriminative power diminishes in deeper layers due to alignment constraints.
The model possesses internal risk awareness that is not consistently translated into its language output.
SASA reduces ASR by an average of 97% using only 5% of data, with minimal degradation of helpfulness.
SASA exhibits remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on previously unseen datasets.
future_direction: Future work could explore extending SASA to other modalities and tasks, and investigating the interplay between safety and other model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to harmful input compared to their language-only backbones. We investigated this vulnerability by exploring LVLMs internal dynamics, framing their inherent safety understanding in terms of three key capabilities. Specifically, we define these capabilities as safety perception, semantic understanding, and alignment for linguistic expression, and experimentally pinpointed their primary locations within the model architecture. The results indicate that safety perception often emerges before comprehensive semantic understanding, leading to the reduction in safety. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA)}, a technique that projects informative semantic representations from intermediate layers onto earlier safety-oriented layers. This approach leverages the model's inherent semantic understanding to enhance safety recognition without fine-tuning. Then, we employ linear probing to articulate the model's internal semantic comprehension to detect the risk before the generation process. Extensive experiments on various datasets and tasks demonstrate that SASA significantly improves the safety of LVLMs, with minimal impact on the utility.

papers.title: SteeringSafety: A Systematic Safety Evaluation Framework of Representation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do representation steering methods affect various safety perspectives, and what are the entanglement patterns when steering for specific safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEERINGSAFETY, a framework for systematic evaluation of representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives, revealing that steering effectiveness and entanglement depend on method-model-perspective pairings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation steering methods exhibit complex entanglement patterns, and a holistic safety evaluation is necessary to understand and mitigate unintended side effects.
papers.key_findings:
DIM and ACE are generally effective for harmfulness and bias steering, while PCA and LAT are promising for hallucination in certain models.
Entanglement is model-dependent but consistently highest for social behaviors and normative judgment, while reasoning remains robust.
Different steering methods targeting the same behavior can create steering vectors entangling distinct perspectives.
Conditional steering enables better effectiveness-entanglement tradeoffs for most perspectives but cannot completely mitigate entanglement.
Jailbreaking doesn't necessarily increase toxicity, hallucination steering causes opposing political shifts across models, and improving one bias type can degrade another.
papers.limitation:
Focus on English-language datasets and instruction-tuned models
Steering is implemented as static vectors applied at fixed model locations, overlooking more adaptive methods
Results are reported in aggregate, potentially obscuring nuanced shifts within behavioral subtypes
future_direction: Expand framework to incorporate weight modifications and other representation engineering approaches
Investigate reasoning models and steering from tokens other than final post-instruction tokens
Generalize findings to other model deployment settings, such as agentic safety and security
papers.abstract: We introduce SteeringSafety, a systematic framework for evaluating representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives spanning 17 datasets. While prior work highlights general capabilities of representation steering, we systematically explore safety perspectives including bias, harmfulness, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. Our framework provides modularized building blocks for state-of-the-art steering methods, enabling unified implementation of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements like conditional steering. Results on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B reveal that strong steering performance depends critically on pairing of method, model, and specific perspective. DIM shows consistent effectiveness, but all methods exhibit substantial entanglement: social behaviors show highest vulnerability (reaching degradation as high as 76%), jailbreaking often compromises normative judgment, and hallucination steering unpredictably shifts political views. Our findings underscore the critical need for holistic safety evaluations.

papers.title: Safety Alignment via Constrained Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving useful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), a safety alignment method that identifies and fixes knowledge-related neurons in MLP layers during unlearning to remove harmful knowledge while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: CKU effectively enhances LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving general capabilities, offering a promising approach for safety alignment and knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
CKU achieves a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods like RSFT, GAM, Eraser, Safe Unlearning, and Circuit Break.
Fixing 80% of neurons (Neuron Locking Rate=0.8) during unlearning yields the greatest safety improvement.
Unlearning applied only to a subset of MLP layers (layers 8-12) results in a fourfold increase in safety with only a 0.15% reduction in utility.
The neuron selection mechanism based on SNIP scoring is more effective than random selection for preserving utility during unlearning.
The unlearning regularization parameter λ controls the safety-utility trade-off, with λ=1.5 providing an optimal balance.
papers.limitation:
CKU's effectiveness varies across different domains or datasets.
CKU may occasionally struggle to provide nuanced explanations in highly complex or ambiguous contexts.
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks. Existing defense mechanisms have not fully deleted harmful knowledge in LLMs, which allows such attacks to bypass safeguards and produce harmful outputs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel safety alignment strategy, Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), which focuses on two primary objectives: knowledge localization and retention, and unlearning harmful knowledge. CKU works by scoring neurons in specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers to identify a subset U of neurons associated with useful knowledge. During the unlearning process, CKU prunes the gradients of neurons in U to preserve valuable knowledge while effectively mitigating harmful content. Experimental results demonstrate that CKU significantly enhances model safety without compromising overall performance, offering a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods. Additionally, our analysis of neuron knowledge sensitivity across various MLP layers provides valuable insights into the mechanics of safety alignment and model knowledge editing.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: The Side Effects of Being Smart: Safety Risks in MLLMs' Multi-Image Reasoning
papers.research_question: Do improved capabilities in multi-image reasoning expand the attack surface and introduce new safety risks in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark for evaluating multi-image reasoning safety in MLLMs, and finds that models with stronger multi-image reasoning capabilities are often more vulnerable to safety attacks, with unsafe generations exhibiting lower attention entropy.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces MIR-SafetyBench and demonstrates extensive safety risks in MLLMs during multi-image reasoning, highlighting the need for improved safety alignment in complex multimodal scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-image relational attacks succeed widely across 19 MLLMs, with the highest Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaching 87.63%.
Within a broad range of models, stronger multi-image reasoning capability correlates with higher ASR, indicating a capability-safety trade-off.
Many safe responses are superficial, arising from misunderstanding, generic refusals, or evasive answers rather than robust safety alignment.
In multi-image scenarios, unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average, suggesting models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints.
Multi-image relational prompts lead to significantly higher ASR compared to single-image prompts for the same harmful intent.
papers.limitation:
Benchmark coverage is not exhaustive and may inherit biases from source datasets and the automated pipeline.
Dependence on automatic components (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, FLUX.1-dev, HarmBench classifier) may introduce systematic noise.
Evaluation is limited to a fixed set of models under single-turn prompting, and attention-entropy analysis provides only correlational evidence.
The work is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, with no concrete mitigation mechanisms proposed.
future_direction: Extend MIR-SafetyBench to more realistic user interactions, additional modalities and relation types, and richer measurements of internal states and real-world safety impact.
Bridge the gap from characterization to practical mitigation with detection mechanisms, safety monitors, or training-time regularizers.
papers.abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) acquire stronger reasoning capabilities to handle complex, multi-image instructions, this advancement may pose new safety risks. We study this problem by introducing MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark focused on multi-image reasoning safety, which consists of 2,676 instances across a taxonomy of 9 multi-image relations. Our extensive evaluations on 19 MLLMs reveal a troubling trend: models with more advanced multi-image reasoning can be more vulnerable on MIR-SafetyBench. Beyond attack success rates, we find that many responses labeled as safe are superficial, often driven by misunderstanding or evasive, non-committal replies. We further observe that unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average. This internal signature suggests a possible risk that models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thu-coai/MIR-SafetyBench.

papers.title: Soteria: Language-Specific Functional Parameter Steering for Multilingual Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we ensure consistent safety across multiple languages in large language models by locating and minimally adjusting language-specific functional parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Soteria, a lightweight method that identifies and adjusts language-specific functional attention heads to improve multilingual safety alignment by modifying only ~3% of parameters, reducing harmful outputs without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: Soteria provides an effective, parameter-efficient path to scalable multilingual safety alignment, enhancing model safety across diverse languages without compromising utility.
papers.key_findings:
Soteria significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages on safety benchmarks like MultiJail and XThreatBench.
The method outperforms baseline safety alignment techniques such as Safety Arithmetic, Resta, and TIES.
Modifying only the O-projection weights of identified functional heads preserves general model capabilities, as shown by stable MMLU scores.
Attention head analysis reveals that high- and mid-resource languages share functional heads in mid-layers, while low-resource languages utilize heads in later layers.
The approach is robust against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks like POATE and RDR.
papers.limitation:
Relies on per-language functional neuron identification, which requires accurate language segmentation and task-based data in each target language; resource constraints and data limitations can reduce selection precision.
Does not guarantee comprehensive coverage of every cultural nuance or emergent harmful behavior.
future_direction: Investigating attention-head analysis to tackle task-specific heads, misalignment, and hallucination issues.
Enhancing universal attention heads to improve cross-lingual understanding and zero-shot performance for underrepresented languages.
Refining or shifting the latent space of problematic heads to improve overall alignment and trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Ensuring consistent safety across multiple languages remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs). We introduce Soteria, a lightweight yet powerful strategy that locates and minimally adjusts the "functional heads" most responsible for harmful content generation in each language. By altering only a fraction of parameters, Soteria drastically reduces policy violations without sacrificing overall model performance, even in low-resource settings. To rigorously evaluate our approach, we also present XThreatBench, a specialized multilingual dataset capturing fine-grained harmful behaviors drawn from real policy guidelines. Experiments with leading open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral) show that Soteria consistently improves safety metrics across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. These findings highlight a promising path toward scalable, linguistically attuned, and ethically aligned LLMs worldwide.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: SafeMERGE: Preserving Safety Alignment in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models via Selective Layer-Wise Model Merging
papers.research_question: How can practitioners retain task utility while improving safety, without relying on custom algorithms, and while using standard open-source libraries?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SafeMERGE, a lightweight post-fine-tuning framework that selectively merges fine-tuned LoRA layers with safety-aligned layers based on cosine similarity, restoring safety without compromising task utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeMERGE is an effective method for restoring safety in fine-tuned LLMs without sacrificing performance, establishing selective layer-wise merging as a robust strategy.
papers.key_findings:
SafeMERGE consistently reduces harmfulness while maintaining or improving task utility across multiple models and tasks.
Selective layer-wise merging outperforms baselines like SafeLoRA, RESTA, and SafeInstruct in terms of safety-utility trade-off.
Cosine similarity is a more reliable metric than Euclidean distance for identifying unsafe layers.
The optimal cosine similarity threshold τ is stable across models and tasks, typically around 0.6-0.8.
Linear merging is sufficient and robust compared to other merging strategies like TIES.
papers.limitation:
Model and task selection is limited to four LLMs and two main tasks, with additional telecom tasks in appendix.
Safety evaluations rely on classifier-based assessment (Llama-Guard-3-8B) which has inherent limitations.
SafeMERGE requires an additional safe model fine-tuned on safety data.
The method is not evaluated against jailbreak-style adversarial attacks.
future_direction: Investigating domain-specific safety datasets for safe model training.
Deeper analysis of TIES merging behavior.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is a common practice to adapt generalist models to specialized domains. However, recent studies show that fine-tuning can erode safety alignment, causing LLMs to respond to harmful or unethical prompts. Many methods to realign safety have been proposed, but often introduce custom algorithms that are difficult to implement or compromise task utility. In this work, we propose SafeMERGE, a lightweight, post-fine-tuning framework that preserves safety while maintaining downstream performance. SafeMERGE selectively merges fine-tuned with safety-aligned model layers only when they deviate from safe behavior, measured by a cosine similarity criterion. Across three LLMs and two tasks, SafeMERGE consistently reduces harmful outputs compared to other defenses, with negligible or even positive impact on utility. Our results demonstrate that selective layer-wise merging offers an effective safeguard against the inadvertent loss of safety during fine-tuning, establishing SafeMERGE as a simple post-fine-tuning defense.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Antidote: Post-fine-tuning Safety Alignment for Large Language Models against Harmful Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: Is there a defense that can be less sensitive to the hyper-parameters of the fine-tuning stage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Antidote, a post-fine-tuning defense that prunes harmful weights to recover model safety, which is agnostic to fine-tuning hyper-parameters and reduces harmful score while maintaining downstream task accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Antidote provides an effective post-fine-tuning safety alignment solution that mitigates harmful fine-tuning attacks by pruning harmful parameters, addressing the hyper-parameter sensitivity of prior defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Existing alignment-stage and fine-tuning-stage defenses are highly sensitive to fine-tuning hyper-parameters (learning rate, epochs), a weakness termed the hyper-parameter sensitivity issue.
Antidote, a one-shot pruning method applied after fine-tuning, effectively reduces harmful scores across various harmful data ratios and fine-tuning settings.
Antidote maintains downstream task accuracy close to the undefended baseline while significantly improving safety.
The method generalizes across different model architectures (Llama2, Mistral, Gemma) and is compatible with stronger safety alignment datasets.
Antidote introduces minimal system overhead compared to other defense methods, mainly from calculating the Wanda score.
papers.limitation: Requires access to a separate harmful dataset (re-alignment dataset) for calculating the pruning mask.
future_direction: Exploring model acceleration benefits from the pruning step.
Extending the method to more advanced models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Safety aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to harmful fine-tuning attacks -- a few harmful data mixed in the fine-tuning dataset can break the LLMs's safety alignment. While several defenses have been proposed, our evaluation shows that existing defenses fail \textit{when some specific training hyper-parameters are chosen} -- a large learning rate or a large number of training epochs in the fine-tuning stage can easily invalidate the defense. To this end, we propose Antidote, a post-fine-tuning stage solution, which remains \textbf{\textit{agnostic to the training hyper-parameters in the fine-tuning stage}}. Antidote relies on the philosophy that by removing the harmful parameters, the harmful model can be recovered from the harmful behaviors, regardless of how those harmful parameters are formed in the fine-tuning stage. With this philosophy, we introduce a one-shot pruning stage after harmful fine-tuning to remove the harmful weights that are responsible for the generation of harmful content. Despite its embarrassing simplicity, empirical results show that Antidote can reduce harmful score while maintaining accuracy on downstream tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/git-disl/Antidote.

papers.title: Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cross-lingual safety alignment in LLMs, specifically identifying a sparse set of shared safety neurons that regulate safety behavior across languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a sparse set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons) that regulate safety behavior across languages and proposes a neuron-oriented training strategy that selectively fine-tunes these neurons to improve safety in low-resource languages without degrading general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cross-lingual safety alignment can be achieved by identifying and selectively fine-tuning a sparse set of shared safety neurons, which improves safety in low-resource languages while minimizing the alignment tax.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) that are causally responsible for safety refusal behavior.
The subset of MS-Neurons shared between high-resource and low-resource languages (SS-Neurons) serves as a bridge for cross-lingual safety transfer.
Suppressing SS-Neurons causes concurrent safety drops across low-resource languages, while reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency.
The proposed SS-Neuron expansion strategy, which fine-tunes only the English MS-Neurons using parallel safety data, significantly reduces attack success rates in low-resource languages while preserving model utility.
The method is parameter-efficient, updating less than 0.6% of parameters, and outperforms state-of-the-art safety alignment methods.
papers.limitation: The study primarily focuses on safety-oriented tasks, and the applicability to general-purpose tasks remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validate the neuron-level intervention across non-safety domains to transfer complex cognitive skills.
papers.abstract: Multilingual safety remains significantly imbalanced, leaving non-high-resource (NHR) languages vulnerable compared to robust high-resource (HR) ones. Moreover, the neural mechanisms driving safety alignment remain unclear despite observed cross-lingual representation transfer. In this paper, we find that LLMs contain a set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons), a remarkably small yet critical neuronal subset that jointly regulates safety behavior across languages. We first identify monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) and validate their causal role in safety refusal behavior through targeted activation and suppression. Our cross-lingual analyses then identify SS-Neurons as the subset of MS-Neurons shared between HR and NHR languages, serving as a bridge to transfer safety capabilities from HR to NHR domains. We observe that suppressing these neurons causes concurrent safety drops across NHR languages, whereas reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency. Building on these insights, we propose a simple neuron-oriented training strategy that targets SS-Neurons based on language resource distribution and model architecture. Experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning this tiny neuronal subset outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly enhancing NHR safety while maintaining the model's general capabilities. The code and dataset will be available athttps://github.com/1518630367/SS-Neuron-Expansion.

papers.title: SafeSteer: Interpretable Safety Steering with Refusal-Evasion in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model outputs for safety at inference time without fine-tuning, using activation steering with category-specific vectors?
papers.core_contribution: SAFE STEER enables precise, customizable safety adjustments in LLMs through category-specific steering vectors computed from activations, without fine-tuning or contrastive data, while maintaining text quality.
papers.conclusion: SAFE STEER demonstrates effective inference-time safety steering across LLMs and datasets, providing precise control, preventing blanket refusals, and guiding models to generate safe, contextually relevant content.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE STEER reduces the percentage of unsafe responses in LLMs across various harm categories.
It effectively uses generic safe data without requiring contrastive paired datasets.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves steering signals and safety outcomes.
The method outperforms baselines like SEA and CAA in safety and utility metrics.
Steering maintains or improves text quality attributes such as helpfulness and coherence while enhancing safety.
future_direction: Investigate transferability of steering vectors across models and categories.
Scale up the method to more harm categories and models for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to adapt to evolving safety policies is costly and impractical.
